reran: cmd.sh on w3-int, w3-base and 2.13.18: compiles and prints 'false 3' on all three. 2.12.20 rejects both arguments with 'annotation argument needs to be a constant'. 3.7.4 reports two errors.
user_impact: No one writes a block as an annotation argument. The same check also accepts any expression whose type is a literal type: `def three(): 3 = { println(..); 3 }` then `@Ann(i = K.three())`, `@Ann(i = K.four)` for `val four: 4`, and `@Ann(i = id(5))` for `def id[T <: Singleton](t: T): T` all compile and store 3, 4, 5 without evaluating anything. The stored value is the one the type guarantees, so nothing wrong is computed; what is lost is an error, and a reader's expectation that the expression runs.
fixability: design question: whether an annotation argument may be any expression of literal type or must be a constant expression in the sense of SLS 6.24. If the second, tryConst (Typers.scala around line 4102) should require a Literal or a tree that is safe to fold, at the cost of rejecting source that 2.13.0 to 2.13.18 accept.
regression: in 2.13.0: literal types (SIP-23, commit 2cdd67e546) give `{ stats; 3 }` and calls of literal-typed methods a ConstantType, which tryConst has accepted in place of a literal tree since 2011 (commit b2ca0efb2d). 2.12.20 rejects the reproduction.
links: EO6 and LZ2 (retronym/scala PR 606) are the neighbouring case in ordinary code. PR 606 changes when typedBlock gives a block a foldable constant type; it does not touch tryConst, which reads the type of any tree, and the finding is present on the integration build that includes 606. The right outcome is a separate change to tryConst, not a wider 606. R1 and R2 (pickling of blocks in annotation arguments) are about Scala StaticAnnotations and unrelated.
note: Specification: SLS 11 says a ConstantAnnotation 'may only have arguments which are constant expressions' and links SLS 6.24, whose list (literals, classOf, platform enum elements, literal arrays, constant value definitions) has no block and no method call, though it is worded 'at least'. Scala 3.7.4 rejects every form above for a Java annotation ('Annotation argument is not a constant'); it does not check a Scala ConstantAnnotation at all, so `@C({ K.side(); 3 })` for `class C(i: Int) extends ConstantAnnotation` and `@deprecated({ K.side(); "msg" }, "1.0")` compile in both. The hunter's framing as dropped side effects overstates it: annotation arguments are never evaluated, so the only defect is the missing error. The hunter's point about macros and inline helpers is speculative.
